title: Jackfruit Latex and Pomegranate Peel: An Unlikely Recipe for Regrowing Gum Tissue
summary: Periodontitis is a chronic inflammatory disease that erodes the bone and ligaments anchoring your teeth. Standard treatments control infection but do little to regenerate lost tissue. Now, scientists at the Pontifical Catholic University of São Paulo have developed an unusual biomaterial that could change that: a sticky gel combining jackfruit latex, pomegranate peel extract, and the statin drug simvastatin. 'We began to view latex extracted from jackfruit as an interesting alternative, as it has adhesive properties,' explained Professor Eliana Aparecida de Rezende Duek, who coordinated the study published in Polymer Bulletin. The latex forms a mucoadhesive matrix that clings to damaged periodontal tissue, allowing targeted, sustained release of therapeutic compounds. Pomegranate peel brings topical antimicrobial action, while simvastatin—a drug normally taken orally for cholesterol—has shown bone-stimulating effects. Delivering simvastatin locally could also bypass a major drawback: when swallowed, most of the drug is trapped by the liver, requiring high doses that risk muscle degeneration. In lab tests, the team incorporated simvastatin at 0.3%, 0.6%, and 1.2% concentrations without disrupting the gel's structure. They then exposed human adipose-derived stem cells to the material. All three concentrations triggered osteoinduction—the process that nudges stem cells to become bone-forming cells—within 14 days, with even stronger results at 21 days. 'Overall, the results were very encouraging,' Duek said. 'The developed biomaterial has great potential for future applications in treating periodontitis and in other areas as well.' However, she stressed that further studies are needed to thoroughly evaluate safety and efficacy before clinical use. If successful, this tropical-fruit-based gel could offer a regenerative option for millions suffering from severe gum disease—and perhaps inspire similar approaches for bone repair elsewhere.
why_it_matters: Dental health issues like periodontitis can lead to tooth loss and affect overall health; a treatment that actually regrows bone would be life-changing. It also shows how everyday natural substances can be transformed into advanced medical therapies through creative science.

background_read: Periodontitis affects nearly half of adults over 30 in some countries, making it one of the most common chronic diseases. Regular treatments like deep cleaning and surgery can stop the infection but rarely rebuild lost bone, leaving teeth loose and at risk. Biomaterials science has been exploring natural polymers—such as latex from rubber trees and fruit—as scaffolds for tissue repair because they are biocompatible and sustainable. Simvastatin, first approved in the 1990s to lower cholesterol, was later found to have bone-forming side effects, sparking interest in using it for orthopedic and dental applications. The Pontifical Catholic University of São Paulo (a major research university in Brazil) led this study, combining these three components into a single gel. Pomegranate peel is rich in compounds that fight bacteria, adding another layer of protection to the gum tissue. While promising, the gel still has to pass rigorous safety and clinical trials before dentists can use it, a process that can take many years.

perspectives.description: For patients, a painless, regenerative gel could mean fewer surgeries, saved teeth, and lower long-term costs, especially in regions with limited access to specialized dental care.

The gel is still in early testing; latex allergies and potential side effects from simvastatin need careful study, and growing jackfruit for medical latex could have environmental implications if not managed sustainably.

Combining natural products with a repurposed drug exemplifies how biomaterials research bridges traditional medicine and modern pharmacology, tapping into plants that have been used for centuries in folk remedies.

If successful, this approach could be adapted to repair bone in the spine, hips, or jaw, and might encourage the development of other plant-based gels for tissue engineering—leading to a new generation of affordable, biocompatible medical products.
